context.text: Kyiv is where the Orthodoxy of the eastern Slavs began. From the baptism of Rus in 988, the metropolia of Kyiv belonged to the Church of Constantinople; only in 1686, with the city under Muscovite rule, did a synodal letter of Patriarch Dionysius IV permit Moscow to ordain Kyiv's metropolitan. Whether that letter transferred the church of Ukraine to Moscow forever, or merely delegated its administration, is the disputed root of everything that follows: Moscow reads it one way, Constantinople the other, and both have read it their own way for over three hundred years.

The twentieth century left the Ukrainian church broken into pieces. A Ukrainian Autocephalous Orthodox Church, born in 1921, survived persecution and exile. In 1990 Moscow granted its Ukrainian exarchate self-government as the Ukrainian Orthodox Church, the UOC. After Ukraine's independence, Metropolitan Filaret (Denisenko) of Kyiv sought full autocephaly from Moscow; refused, he was deposed at the Kharkiv council of 1992 and anathematized in 1997, and founded the Ukrainian Orthodox Church of the Kyiv Patriarchate. For a quarter century, Ukraine held one canonical church in communion with world Orthodoxy through Moscow, and two large bodies recognized by no one, together numbering millions of baptized faithful: the largest unhealed schism in the Orthodox world.

The church question was never merely canonical. It was entangled with the question of Ukrainian nationhood from the beginning, and Russia's annexation of Crimea and the war in the Donbas after 2014 fused the two. President Petro Poroshenko made autocephaly a cause of state, campaigning under the slogan of army, language, and faith, and in April 2018 he and the Ukrainian parliament formally petitioned Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew for a tomos. That a head of state should petition for autocephaly startled many; it also had precedent, for it was the tsar's government that had pressed Constantinople into recognizing Moscow's own patriarchate in 1589.

narrative.text: Constantinople took up the petition through 2018: exarchs were appointed to Kyiv in September, and on October 11 its Holy Synod resolved to proceed to autocephaly, re-established its stavropegion in Kyiv, received the appeals of Filaret and of Makariy Maletych of the UAOC, restoring them and their followers to rank and communion, and revoked the binding force of the 1686 letter. Moscow answered on October 15 by breaking eucharistic communion with Constantinople, the schism treated in its own account on this timeline.

On December 15, 2018, a unification council met in the cathedral of Holy Wisdom, St Sophia in Kyiv. The Kyiv Patriarchate and the UAOC dissolved themselves into a new body, the Orthodox Church of Ukraine, the OCU, and elected as primate the thirty-nine-year-old Metropolitan Epifaniy (Dumenko). Of the UOC's roughly ninety bishops, two took part; the rest stayed away, their bishops' council having ruled the whole process anti-canonical the month before.

On January 5, 2019, in the patriarchal cathedral of St George at the Phanar, Patriarch Bartholomew signed the Patriarchal and Synodal Tomos of autocephaly, and on January 6 he placed it in Epifaniy's hands. Its terms mark the OCU's place in the Orthodox family: a metropolitanate, not a patriarchate, ranked last in the diptychs; holy chrism received from Constantinople; its diaspora ceded to the Ecumenical Throne; and the right of final appeal reserved to Constantinople.

Recognition then divided the Orthodox world. The Ecumenical Patriarchate was joined by the Patriarchate of Alexandria, the Church of Greece, and the Church of Cyprus; the remaining local churches either rejected the tomos or have taken no formal position, and the Moscow Patriarchate broke or restricted communion with each church that recognized it. Filaret himself, honorary patriarch in the new church, repudiated its terms within months and attempted to revive the Kyiv Patriarchate in June 2019, taking a small following with him.

The UOC, still the largest church in Ukraine by number of parishes, walked its own hard road. When Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022 and Patriarch Kirill of Moscow blessed it, the UOC's council at Feofaniya on May 27, 2022 condemned the war as a violation of the commandment against murder, declared its disagreement with Kirill, and struck every clause of subordination to Moscow from its statute, declaring its full self-sufficiency and independence. It did not pronounce the word autocephaly, and Moscow continues to list it as its own autonomous branch; its precise canonical status has been argued about ever since, inside the UOC as much as outside it.

The Ukrainian state pressed the question further. Parish transfers from the UOC to the OCU, running into the thousands since 2019, have been celebrated as free self-determination on one side and denounced as raider seizures on the other, and some were violent. Security services searched UOC monasteries and chanceries; several hierarchs were sanctioned or prosecuted; the UOC's presence in the Kyiv Caves Lavra was terminated. In August 2024 Ukraine adopted law 3894-IX, banning religious organizations affiliated with the Russian Orthodox Church, with a procedure aimed at the UOC. Kyiv defends these measures as wartime national security; UN human rights monitors and others have raised religious-freedom concerns about them. Both things can be documented; readers will weigh them differently.

significance.text: Autocephaly, a local church's right to govern itself and elect its own head, is Orthodoxy's ancient way of becoming at home in a nation. What the Ukrainian case exposed is that Orthodoxy has no agreed procedure for granting it: the pan-Orthodox preparatory process of the twentieth century drafted rules but never ratified them, and Crete in 2016 left the document unfinished. Constantinople acted on its historic prerogative as the Mother Church; Moscow called the act a raid on its canonical territory. Every unresolved question of Orthodox order, primacy, appeals, territory, and the diaspora, surfaced at once in Ukraine.
The charge of politics, on both sides

Each church's critics describe the other as a political artifact, and honesty requires stating both charges precisely. The UOC and Moscow call the OCU a project of the Ukrainian state with open Western encouragement. The state's role is documented: Poroshenko petitioned for the tomos, campaigned on it, and toured it through the country, and the United States publicly welcomed and supported the autocephaly in official statements. The stronger form of the charge, that Western intelligence services created the OCU, circulates widely in Russian church and state media; no public evidence has established it, and scholars who have examined the record find loud governmental cheerleading rather than manufacture. The claim is reported here as a claim.

The charge runs the other way with equal force. The OCU and the Ukrainian state describe the UOC as a channel of Russian influence in wartime, pointing to its canonical bond with a patriarchate that blessed the invasion, and individual cases of collaboration have been prosecuted. The UOC answers with its record: it condemned the invasion from the first day, its Feofaniya council broke with Moscow's position and struck subordination from its statute, and its parishes have buried Ukrainian soldiers throughout the war. Here too, the general charge is reported as a charge.

What the slogans obscure is that both churches are made of real parishes, real baptisms, and real faithful, overwhelmingly Ukrainians on both sides of the line. The language of 'fake church', aimed in either direction, describes no one's actual congregation. The division runs through towns, through families, and sometimes through a single parish, and it will not be healed by a communiqué.

consequences.text: The tomos brought millions of Ukrainians from unrecognized bodies into churches in communion with four ancient sees, which its supporters count as the healing of a generation-long schism; it also entrenched a second division, between the OCU and the UOC, and detonated the Moscow–Constantinople schism whose costs all Orthodoxy now bears. As of the mid-2020s the recognition map has not moved since Cyprus in 2020, the UOC's status after Feofaniya remains contested, and the war has made every question sharper. Whether Ukraine's two Orthodox churches end in one local church, and by what path, is among the largest open questions in the Orthodox world.

uncertainty: This entry is marked jurisdiction-specific because the Orthodox churches themselves disagree about it: four local churches recognize the OCU's autocephaly, others reject it, and the UOC's post-2022 status is disputed even among its own theologians. The narrative facts, councils, documents, and dates are public and firm. The competing characterizations of the two churches, including allegations of intelligence-agency involvement on either side, are reported as the positions of those who make them; this entry links each side's own documents and does not adjudicate legitimacy.
